note: demo-video-v2 (Sun Oct 25). Every caption describes what is on screen in that segment; each gameplay shot is used once. Gameplay is the real game in record mode, driven by saved pose landmarks (numbers only, no third-party footage appears). Announcer calls heard in gameplay segments are the game's own stock calls, at the frames the game fired them.

segments.vo: Step toward the camera and your fighter walks in. Jab, hook, then drive a fist up for the super uppercut.
Throw Hands. Your body is the controller.
The best game nights are loud and physical. But motion games need a console, an accessory, and everyone in one room. Your friends are on other campuses, in other cities.
So we built a fighting game that runs in a browser with a webcam. Two friends, two screens, one fight.
A short tutorial teaches movement: step or lean toward the camera to advance, back to retreat, and sideways to circle.
Your fighter really walks: it circles left and right, steps back, and comes forward, always facing the opponent.
Two players, each driving a fighter with their own punches. Every fist reaches its target before the hit lands.
Forearms up raises your guard. It drains with every blocked hit, and when it breaks, you're dizzy.
With a full super meter, cross your forearms above your face. Iron Wall blocks everything and counters the attacker.
A super uppercut near the fence slams your opponent into the cage.
Brawl puts up to eight fighters in the octagon, with a live KO feed. Bots fill the empty spots.
Online, create a room and share the four-letter code. Friends can watch, cheer, and queue up for winner stays on.
Fighter Forge turns one sentence into your own fighter. Meta's Muse Spark writes it, and Muse Image paints the card.
Online wins feed an Elo leaderboard, stored in Tiger Data.

AI is the controller. A pose model runs in your browser, so no video leaves your device. Our gesture engine turns joint angles into punches, guards, and supers. Gemini writes live commentary, and an announcer voice made with ElevenLabs calls the big moments.

We built it with Claude Code. Playwright tests feed real people's movement into headless browsers as a fake webcam and check that both players' screens agree on every tick. Fresh-context reviewers score every visual change. A Vultr server runs the game, and Tiger Data stores the stats.
